references.text: Jacob (Israel) used deceit (דֹּלוֹס / bedrag) to take the blessing from Esau. Jesus' description of Nathanael as a 'true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit' can be seen as a contrast to the patriarch Jacob, who was known for his deception ([ref:1 Mos 27:35|Genesis 27:35]).
Jacob received the name Israel after wrestling with God. Jesus calls Nathanael a true 'Israelite,' which points back to Jacob's new name and identity ([ref:1 Mos 32:28|Genesis 32:28]).

'Blessed is the person whom the Lord does not count as guilty of sin, and who has no deceit in their spirit.' Jesus' description of Nathanael as one without deceit (δόλος) reflects this psalm's ideal of a sincere person ([ref:Sal 32:2|Psalms 32:2]).
'Truly, God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart.' The true Israelite is the one with a pure heart without deceit, as Jesus describes Nathanael ([ref:Sal 73:1|Psalms 73:1]).

Regarding the Lord's suffering servant it is said that 'there was no deceit in his mouth.' The expression 'without deceit' (δόλος) links Nathanael's characterization to this prophetic ideal ([ref:Jes 53:9|Isaiah 53:9]).

Zephaniah prophesies about the remnant of Israel: 'They will do no wrong and speak no lies, and there will be no deceitful tongue in their mouth.' Nathanael represents this sincere remnant of Israel ([ref:Sef 3:13|Zephaniah 3:13]).

Philip found Nathanael and told him about Jesus from Nazareth, and Nathanael asked doubtfully if anything good could come from Nazareth. This sets the immediate context for Jesus' meeting with Nathanael ([ref:Joh 1:45-46|John 1:45-46]).

Nathanael asks how Jesus knows him, and Jesus answers that he saw him under the fig tree – something that leads to Nathanael's confession of Jesus as God's Son and King of Israel ([ref:Joh 1:48-49|John 1:48-49]).
Jesus 'knew all' and 'knew what was in man.' His supernatural knowledge of Nathanael's character is an example of this divine insight ([ref:Joh 2:24-25|John 2:24-25]).

Paul writes that 'not all who are from Israel are truly Israel.' Jesus' description of Nathanael as a 'true Israelite' touches on the same theme about what it means to be a genuine Israelite ([ref:Rom 9:6|Romans 9:6]).
Regarding the 144,000 it is said that 'no lie was found in their mouth.' This description of God's true people as without deceit reflects Jesus' words about Nathanael ([ref:Åp 14:5|Revelation 14:5]).
